cefr.bandName: Pre-A1, before any English at all

unit.unitOverview:
New sounds: m, c, k.
Three more letters, and two of them share a sound.
Say the sound, not the letter name.
Join the sounds and read the word.
unit.learningPath:
Listen to the lesson.
Words: the new sounds and the new words.
Patterns: the sounds, blending, and writing.
Read three short texts.
Read out loud. Record it.
Write the letters and the words.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
functions: Say the sound each new letter makes
Join sounds together to read a word
Break a word into sounds to write it
Read the new words out loud
Read the common words that phonics cannot sound out

visual.lectureScript:
This is Unit 5. Three more letters.
First. mmm. Close your lips and hum.
Say it with me. mmm. mmm.
Feel your lips touch. That is m.
Next. c. At the back of your mouth. c.
Say it with me. c. c. c.
Last. k. Listen carefully.
k. Say it with me. k. k.
Did you hear? c and k are the same sound.
Two letters. One sound.
That is normal in English. It is not a mistake.
Cat starts with c. Kit starts with k.
The sound is the same. The letter is not.
You will learn which one to use by reading.
Now join them.
c. a. t. Cat.
Say it with me. c-a-t. Cat.
Another. mmm. a. p. Map.
And. k. i. t. Kit.
Now three tricky words.
The first is old. The second is no. The third is so.
All three say oh, not the sound in dog.
Learn all three by sight today.
Now try the sounds on am. a. m. Am.
It works. The word am is not tricky. I am here.
That is Unit 5.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: The new sounds: m, c, k
grammar.explanation:
Each letter makes one sound.
Say the SOUND, not the letter name.
The name comes later and does not help you read.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
m   as in m
c   as in c
k   as in k
grammar.workedExample:
You see the letter m.
1. Do not say its name.
2. Say its sound.
3. Say it two or three times.
4. Now find it in a word.
5. Say the sound again in the word.
grammar.commonMistake:
Saying the letter NAME breaks blending.
Em-ay-pee will never make map.
Mmm-aaa-p makes map.
grammar.practice:
Say the sound for each one.
1. m
2. c
3. k
grammar.answerKey:
Check yourself out loud.
Did you say a sound and not a name?
All right? Go on to the blending card.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Joining m, c, k into words
grammar.explanation:
This is reading.
Say each sound, then run them together.
Slow first. Fast comes on its own.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
c - a - t      ->  cat
m - a - p      ->  map
k - i - t      ->  kit
m - u - m      ->  mum

c and k make the same sound.
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word cat.
1. Say the first sound.
2. Say the next.
3. Say the last.
4. Now run them together, faster.
5. That is the word.
grammar.commonMistake:
c and k are the same sound.
You cannot hear which one a word uses.
You learn that by reading the word.
grammar.practice:
Join the sounds and write the word.
1. c - a - t
2. m - a - p
3. k - i - t
4. m - u - m
5. c - a - n
6. c - a - p
grammar.answerKey:
1. cat
2. map
3. kit
4. mum
5. can
6. cap
Five or six right? You can read these.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Writing words with m, c, k
grammar.explanation:
Reading is joining. Writing is the other way.
Say the word. Break it into sounds. Write each one.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
cat  ->  c - a - t  ->  write c, then a, then t

Say it.
Count the sounds.
Write one letter for each sound.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write the word map.
1. Say it out loud.
2. Break it: m - a - p.
3. How many sounds? Count them.
4. Write one letter for each.
5. Read it back to check.
grammar.commonMistake:
Do not remember the word as a picture.
Hear the sounds. Write one letter for each.
grammar.memoryTip: Say it, count it, write it, read it back.
grammar.practice:
Write the word you hear.
1. kit
2. mum
3. can
4. cap
5. mat
6. kid
grammar.answerKey:
1. kit
2. mum
3. can
4. cap
5. mat
6. kid
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Tricky words: old, no, so
grammar.explanation:
Some words do not follow the sounds.
You cannot work them out. You learn them by sight.
There are not many, and they are the commonest words.
grammar.workedExample:
You meet the word old.
1. Try the sounds first. Always try first.
2. It does not work.
3. So this is a tricky word.
4. Look at it. Say it. Look away. Say it.
5. Do that three times today.
grammar.commonMistake:
Do not guess from the first letter.
Look at the whole word, then say it.
grammar.practice:
Read these out loud, by sight.
1. old
2. no
3. so
grammar.answerKey:
There is no working out here.
Check: did you read each one without stopping?
Not yet? Look, say, look away, say. Three times a day.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.note: This is the rule the whole level rests on and the one adults break most, because many of them half-know the alphabet already. Em-ay-pee will never make map. Correct it every single time, kindly, and say why.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Blending is a motor skill, not a fact
teacherNotes.note: A learner who understands blending perfectly still cannot do it until they have done it a few hundred times. Repetition here is not remediation; it is the lesson. Keep the pace up and come back tomorrow.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Tricky words are taught, not worked out
teacherNotes.note: Try the sounds first, always — most English words do follow them. When they do not, the move is look, say, look away, say, three times a day. Do not let a learner grind at a word that cannot be decoded.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Two letters, one sound — say it before they ask
teacherNotes.note: This is the first time English stops being one letter one sound, and a learner who notices it on their own often decides they have misunderstood something. Name it: c and k are the same sound, English simply has two letters for it, and which word takes which is learned by reading rather than by rule.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: m and n get confused by ear, not by eye
teacherNotes.note: Both are hums. The difference is the lips: m closes them, n does not. Have the learner put a finger on their lips and say both.
